migrationNotes: Spine: follow a scribe's slips into the copying of DNA, learn to find a slip by comparing a copy with its original, ask which slips can reach a child, and end on how chance supplies variants and selection sorts them.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): bio-mutation-and-variation-hook, -6 and -which-info. The scribe's rate is worked in the first teaching screen; -6 repeats the comparison skill of -2 and the skill check; -which-info is covered in the prose after the comparison figure.

lesson.title: Where does a new variant come from?

lead.text: Copying slips have a name. A mutation is a change in the order of bases in DNA. A cell's slips come in the same kinds as the scribe's. One base can be swapped for another, which is called a substitution. A base can be added, which is an insertion, and a base can be left out, which is a deletion.

A substitution replaces one base with another, so the length of the DNA stays the same: a gene of 600 bases is still 600 bases long afterwards. Insertions and deletions change the length. Cells copy with great care and repair most slips, but copying errors and damage to DNA both happen, and neither happens for a reason. A mutation arises by chance, in the way a typing slip does.

The scribe's rate gives the idea of scale. At one slip in every 100 words, a page of 500 words carries on average 500 ÷ 100 = 5 slips. Biologists make the same kind of calculation for DNA: how many changes should turn up in this many bases at this rate.
Look at which base changed and what stayed the same.

To find a mutation you compare the copy with the original. Write the two sequences one above the other so that they line up, and compare them position by position from the left. Wherever the two bases match, nothing has changed. Wherever they differ, that base has changed.

Take ACGT and AGGT. The first pair is A and A, which matches. The second pair is C and G, which differs. The last two pairs match again. Exactly one position differs, so one base has changed: a C became a G, which is a substitution.

afterFigure.text: Finding a changed base shows only that the DNA has changed. It says nothing about what the change does. Some changes damage a protein badly, some alter it slightly and some have no noticeable effect, and telling which needs evidence about the organism as well as the sequence.

lead.text: Compare the two sequences position by position, and count only the pairs that disagree.

Not every mutation can be passed on. A mutation lives in the cell where it happens and in the cells that descend from that cell by mitosis. A mutation in a skin cell is copied into the skin cells that grow from it and stays in that one body. When the person has children, it does not go with them.

A child inherits only what is in the gametes that made it. A mutation in the line of cells that make eggs or sperm can end up in a gamete. If that gamete takes part in fertilisation, every cell of the child carries the change, because every cell descends from that first cell. The parents need not carry the change anywhere else in their bodies. This is how a new allele can enter a family, and eventually a species.
Think about which cells take part in fertilisation.

steps.headline: Chance makes variants, selection sorts them

lead.text: A mutation does not arise because the organism would benefit from it. Mutations happen by chance, whether the change helps, harms or makes no difference. Most make little or no difference. A few harm, and a very few help in the environment where the organism lives.

What happens next is a separate matter. Suppose a few bacteria in a large group carry a variant that lets them survive an antibiotic. The variant was there before the drug arrived, the result of an earlier chance mutation. When the drug kills the other bacteria, the survivors multiply, and a much larger share of the group now carries the variant. This sorting is called selection: a variant that helps its carriers leave more offspring becomes more common.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows one variant drawn blue and another drawn gold, before and after a sorting like this. Selection changed how common each variant is. The helpful variant was already present, so the environment only decided which ones were left.

lead.text: Think about whether the organism or the environment decides which new variants appear.
After an environmental change, one variant becomes more common in a group of organisms.

lesson.orientation: Distinguish DNA change from directed need and identify what can be inherited.
lesson.reviewLabel: Where does a new variant come from?
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A scribe is copying a page of 500 words by hand. She is careful and she checks her work, but on average she slips once in every 100 words. A slip might swap a letter for another, miss a letter out or write one twice. The copy she hands over is almost the same as the original, and where it differs, nobody told her to change it.

Now think about the instructions inside a cell. Every time a cell divides it copies its DNA, which is a very long page written in four letters, and a human cell holds about six billion of them. Cells check their copies and repair most slips, but over billions of letters a few are bound to get through.

The last lesson used alleles such as A and a as if they had always existed. Each one had to appear for the first time somewhere, and a slip in copying is one way that happens. This lesson looks at those slips: what they look like, how to spot one by comparing a copy with its original, which ones can reach a child and what decides whether a new version spreads.

intro.promise: By the end you'll spot a mutation by comparing sequences and say which mutations can be inherited and why they are not made to order.

recap.keyIdea: A mutation is a chance change in DNA sequence, and only one in a gamete's line of cells can be inherited. Selection sorts variants and does not order them.

blocks.text: You compared sequences position by position and counted the bases that differed, and you saw that a substitution leaves a gene's length alone. You also traced which mutations reach children and saw that selection sorts variants without ordering them.

recap.nextHook: Mutations supply the variants and selection decides which become common. The next lesson starts in a meadow of beetles, where birds find some colours easier to spot than others.

questions.prompt: ATCG changes to ATGG without changing length. Name this type of single-base change.
hints: No base was inserted or removed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The third base was substituted: C became G.

questions.onCorrect: A substitution. One base was swapped for another, so the length stayed the same.

misconceptions.feedback: An insertion or deletion would change the length. Here the length stayed the same.

questions.prompt: Compare AATG with AACG. How many displayed positions differ?
hints: Align the sequences from the left.
Compare each pair of letters in turn.
Count the mismatches.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only position three differs: T became C.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Compare position by position and count only the mismatches.

misconceptions.feedback: The sequences are not identical. Check each pair of letters.
Only one pair of letters disagrees. Check each pair again.

questions.prompt: Name the reproductive cell type that can carry a DNA mutation directly into an offspring at fertilisation.
hints: Ordinary skin cells do not contribute DNA at fertilisation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A contributing gamete can carry a DNA variant into the offspring.

questions.onCorrect: A gamete. Only the egg and sperm pass DNA to the next generation.

misconceptions.feedback: Body cells do not take part in fertilisation. Name the cell that does.

questions.prompt: A useful variant becomes more frequent after an environmental change. Which explanation avoids a directed-mutation error?
hints: Separate where a variant comes from from how it spreads.

acceptedIdeas: Existing heritable variants differed in reproductive success
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Selection can change the frequency of existing variants; need does not direct a specific helpful mutation.

choices.label: Organisms created exactly the mutation they needed
Existing heritable variants differed in reproductive success
Every individual rewrote its DNA on purpose

questions.onCorrect: Variants were already there. Those that helped their carriers leave more offspring became more common.

misconceptions.feedback: Mutations are not made to order. The variant was already present or arose by chance.
Individuals cannot rewrite their DNA to meet a need.

questions.prompt: Compare the aligned sequences TCGATA and TCAACA. How many positions differ?
hints: Keep both sequences aligned.
Check each of the six positions in turn.
Count the mismatched pairs only.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Positions 3 and 5 differ; the other four agree.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Positions 3 and 5 disagree, so two bases have changed.

misconceptions.feedback: There is another mismatch. Check every position.
That is the length of the sequences. Count only the positions that differ.

questions.prompt: A gene has 600 bases. A single substitution changes one of them. How many bases does the mutated gene have?
hints: Does a substitution add or remove any base?
One base is swapped for another.
The length stays as it was.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A substitution swaps one base for another, so the length is unchanged: 600 bases.

questions.onCorrect: 600. A substitution swaps a base without changing the length.

misconceptions.feedback: A substitution does not remove a base. It swaps one.
A substitution does not add a base. It swaps one.

questions.prompt: A mutation arises in one of a parent's skin cells. What is the likely result for the parent's children?
hints: Which cells pass DNA to children?

acceptedIdeas: They do not inherit it, because it is not in a gamete
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A mutation confined to an ordinary body cell generally does not reach offspring.

choices.label: They do not inherit it, because it is not in a gamete
They inherit it only if it is harmful

questions.onCorrect: They do not inherit it. Only a mutation in a gamete's line of cells can be passed on.

misconceptions.feedback: Skin cells do not pass DNA to the next generation.
Harm does not decide inheritance. Which cells carry the mutation does.

questions.prompt: Compare the aligned sequences ACGTAC and TCGAAG. How many positions differ?
hints: Align the sequences and keep them in step.
Compare each of the six pairs in turn.
Count only the pairs that disagree.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Positions 1, 4 and 6 differ; the other three agree.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Positions 1, 4 and 6 differ, so three bases have changed.

misconceptions.feedback: There is another mismatch. Check every position.
That is the length of the sequences. Count only the mismatches.

questions.prompt: How many slips are on the page, on average?
hints: How many hundreds of words are on the page?
There is one slip for each hundred words.
Divide the page length by the words per slip.
questions.onCorrect: 5. Even careful copying makes errors at a steady rate, and copying DNA is no different.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many words go by between slips. Count the slips on the whole page.
That is the slips in a single hundred words. The page has more words than that.

questions.prompt: What can you conclude from a single DNA substitution alone?
hints: A changed letter does not specify a trait.

acceptedIdeas: Its biological effect needs additional evidence
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Effects depend on sequence context and environment; some substitutions have little detectable effect.

choices.label: Its biological effect needs additional evidence

questions.onCorrect: Its effect needs more evidence. A changed base may be harmful, helpful or make no difference.

misconceptions.feedback: Many substitutions have little or no effect, so harm cannot be assumed.
Some help, but a change alone does not show that.

questions.prompt: Do mutations arise because an organism needs them? Answer yes or no.
hints: Think about the scribe's slips. Did the scribe choose them?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mutations arise by chance. Need does not direct them.

questions.onCorrect: No. Mutations arise at random, whether or not they would help.

misconceptions.feedback: Mutations arise by chance. An organism's needs do not steer them.
